questions.q: What is the problem with benchmarking a quantum method against an unoptimized greedy search, as flagged in this lesson's first failure mode?
options: Greedy search is a weak baseline (shown to fail 25% of the time even on a trivial 5-node graph), so beating it doesn't demonstrate an advantage over the strongest realistic classical competition like simulated annealing or tuned solvers
Greedy search is actually a stronger baseline than simulated annealing in every case
Greedy search cannot be implemented on any classical computer
There is no problem with this comparison; greedy search is always an adequate baseline
questions.explain: Lesson 20 demonstrated greedy search getting stuck 25% of the time on a trivial graph -- using it as the classical baseline sets a low bar, so beating it doesn't show a quantum method beats the realistic best-available classical competition.

questions.q: Why does the lesson insist that query count alone (e.g. 'quantum needs 1,000x fewer queries') is not sufficient to establish a practical advantage?
options: Because query count says nothing about per-query cost -- if each quantum query is far slower or noisier than a classical sample, wall-clock time could still favor the classical method
Because query count is always a fabricated number with no mathematical basis
Because classical methods never use queries of any kind
Because quantum computers cannot be benchmarked by query count under any circumstances
questions.explain: This echoes Lesson 16's amplitude estimation discussion: a favorable query-count ratio can be misleading if each query's actual cost (time, noise, overhead) differs dramatically between the two methods -- wall-clock time must be reported too.

questions.q: What does 'same instance, same success criterion' require in a fair quantum-vs-classical benchmark?
options: Both methods must solve the literal same problem instance and be judged against the same explicit, shared standard (e.g. the same approximation-ratio threshold), not different bars for each side
Only the quantum method needs a defined success criterion; the classical method's criterion is irrelevant
The classical and quantum methods may use different problem instances as long as both are 'similar in spirit'
Success criteria do not need to be specified in advance, only after seeing the results
questions.explain: If one method's bar is 'approximation ratio >= 0.9' and the other's is 'provable optimum,' the comparison doesn't actually reveal which method performed better -- a fair benchmark picks one explicit, shared criterion applied identically to both sides.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say timing only the 'quantum part' of a QAOA pipeline, while excluding the classical parameter optimizer's cost, produces an unfair comparison?
options: Because the classical optimizer (potentially running hundreds of circuit evaluations, as in Lesson 8) is a real, necessary part of the full pipeline, and excluding its cost compares an incomplete quantum pipeline against a complete classical one
Because the classical optimizer never actually takes any time to run
Because QAOA pipelines have no classical components at all
Because wall-clock time is never relevant to pipeline benchmarking
questions.explain: A full QAOA pipeline includes QUBO construction, circuit building, and the classical optimizer's iterative search (Lesson 8) -- timing only the quantum circuit execution and ignoring that classical cost gives an unfairly incomplete picture versus a fully-timed classical baseline.

questions.q: According to the lesson's checklist, what four questions should be asked before trusting a quantum-vs-classical optimization benchmark?
options: Is the classical baseline the strongest reasonably available; is the comparison metric clearly specified and applied identically; is the tested problem size representative (not cherry-picked); does the accounting include the full pipeline on both sides?
Was the paper published in a prestigious journal; how many authors contributed; was the code open-sourced; did it use Python or another language?
Did the quantum method use more than 10 qubits; was the experiment run twice; did it mention Chapter 5 by name; was a p-value reported?
Is the result exciting; does it use the word 'quantum advantage'; is it shorter than 5 pages; did a company fund the research?
questions.explain: The lesson's four-point checklist covers baseline strength, explicit shared metrics, representative (non-cherry-picked) problem size, and full end-to-end pipeline accounting -- these are the substantive questions that distinguish a fair benchmark from a misleading one.
